title: AUD U3·W3 — Group Audits, Using the Work of Others & Quality Management
lessonHtml:
Cold open — when one auditor isn't enough

Large or multi-location engagements pull in other people's work — component auditors on a group audit, the client's internal audit function, outside specialists — and every firm operates under a system of quality management that governs how engagements are performed. This week covers how the auditor uses (and remains responsible for) others' work, how the engagement is documented, and the firm-level and engagement-level quality structures that stand behind the opinion.

Group audits

When financial statements include multiple components (subsidiaries, divisions, locations), AU-C 600 governs the group audit. The group engagement team sets group materiality and a lower component materiality, identifies significant components (individually material or carrying significant risks), and directs the work of component auditors. The group engagement partner is responsible for the group opinion. Under current standards the group auditor generally assumes responsibility for the components' work and does not reference the component auditor in the report — and if it cannot obtain sufficient evidence over a significant component, that is a scope limitation.

Communicating with component auditors

The group team's involvement is active: it communicates its requirements to component auditors (materiality, significant risks, timing), evaluates their competence and independence, and reviews their work in proportion to component risk. For a significant component, an audit of the full financial information is performed; for others, the group team may use specified procedures or analytical procedures at the group level. Throughout, the group team retains responsibility for the sufficiency of evidence supporting the group opinion — delegation of work is never delegation of responsibility.

Using internal auditors

A strong internal audit function can make the external audit more efficient under AU-C 610 in two ways: using their work (procedures internal audit already performed) and obtaining direct assistance (internal auditors working under the external auditor's direction). Both require evaluating internal audit's competence and objectivity — objectivity is higher when internal audit reports to the audit committee rather than to management. The external auditor must still perform enough work itself on significant judgments and high-risk areas; it cannot delegate those, preserving sole responsibility for the opinion.

Audit documentation

The audit file is the record of work performed. Under AU-C 230, documentation must be sufficient for an experienced auditor with no prior connection to the engagement to understand the nature, timing, and extent of procedures, the evidence obtained, and the conclusions reached — including who performed and reviewed the work and when. The auditor assembles the final file within a documentation completion period (60 days after the report date for AICPA engagements; 45 for PCAOB) and retains it (5 years AICPA; 7 years PCAOB). After the completion date, documentation may be added but not deleted, with the reason recorded.

Firm-level quality management

Behind every engagement sits the firm's system of quality management (SQM). The AICPA's quality-management standards (SQMS) require a firm to design a risk-based system across components including governance and leadership, the firm's risk-assessment process, relevant ethical requirements, acceptance and continuance of clients, engagement performance, resources, information and communication, and monitoring and remediation. The firm sets quality objectives, identifies quality risks, and designs responses — then evaluates the system at least annually. It is the structural assurance that the firm can consistently perform quality engagements.

Engagement quality reviews

Certain engagements require an engagement quality review (EQR) — an objective evaluation by a qualified reviewer who was not on the engagement team, completed before the report is released. The reviewer assesses the significant judgments and conclusions, particularly on risk and independence. At the engagement level, AU-C 220 makes the engagement partner responsible for overall quality, direction, supervision, and review — the bridge between the firm's system and the individual audit, ensuring quality is delivered where it matters: on the engagement itself.

Putting responsibility in one place

The thread tying this week together is that responsibility does not divide. Whether the auditor relies on a component auditor, internal audit, or a specialist, and however robust the firm's quality system, the engagement partner owns the opinion and must ensure sufficient appropriate evidence supports it. Quality management and documentation are the mechanisms that make that responsibility demonstrable — to a reviewer, a regulator, or a court — long after the report is signed.

Communication with those charged with governance

The auditor must communicate specified matters to those charged with governance (typically the audit committee): the auditor's responsibilities and the planned scope and timing, significant findings (qualitative aspects of accounting practices, significant difficulties encountered, uncorrected misstatements), and any significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in internal control — the latter in writing. The auditor also reports fraud involving senior management and identified illegal acts. These communications, required by AU-C 260 and 265, keep governance informed of matters that bear on its oversight of the financial-reporting process.

Acceptance and continuance

Quality begins before fieldwork, at client acceptance and continuance. The firm evaluates management integrity, its own competence and resources to perform the engagement, and compliance with independence and ethical requirements, and communicates with the predecessor auditor (with the client's permission) about disagreements and the reasons for the change. An engagement the firm should never have accepted is the root of many quality failures, which is why acceptance and continuance is an explicit component of the system of quality management — the gate that keeps unacceptable risk out of the firm.

Monitoring and remediation

A quality system is only as good as its monitoring. The firm performs ongoing and periodic monitoring — including inspection of completed engagements — to detect deficiencies, then evaluates their severity and remediates root causes. Findings from external peer review or PCAOB inspection feed the same loop. This continuous monitor-and-remediate cycle is what makes the system of quality management a living process rather than a binder on a shelf, closing the gap between how engagements are supposed to be performed and how they actually are.

CMA bridge

For a multi-entity construction group like MBG and its affiliates, the group-audit and component-materiality concepts are exactly how a consolidated audit would be scoped. The internal-control and consolidation work from the CMA and FAR units is what a component auditor would test — and what the group team would direct and take responsibility for.

Practice and recap

  1. Scope a group audit: group vs component materiality, significant components, the group partner's responsibility for the opinion (assume responsibility; don't reference component auditors).
  2. Use internal audit (their work + direct assistance) and specialists only after evaluating competence and objectivity; keep high-risk judgments in-house.
  3. Document so an experienced auditor can understand the work; assemble within 60 days (AICPA), retain 5 years (7 for PCAOB).
  4. Apply the firm's risk-based system of quality management (SQMS components) and engagement quality reviews completed before report release.

Recap: group audits set group and component materiality and the group partner owns the opinion (assuming responsibility for component work); internal auditors and specialists may be used after evaluating competence and objectivity, but high-risk judgments stay with the auditor; documentation must let an experienced auditor understand the work and is assembled within 60 days and retained 5–7 years; and a risk-based system of quality management plus engagement quality reviews stand behind every report — with responsibility always resting on the engagement partner.

flashcards.back: Group materiality for the consolidated statements; a lower component materiality for components. Significant components are individually material or carry significant risks.
The group engagement partner is responsible for the group opinion; under current standards the group auditor assumes responsibility and does NOT reference component auditors in the report.
Two modes: using their work and direct assistance. Both require evaluating competence and objectivity (higher when IA reports to the audit committee).
Enough for an experienced auditor with no prior connection to understand nature/timing/extent, evidence, conclusions, and who did/reviewed the work and when.
Assemble final file within 60 days (AICPA) / 45 (PCAOB); retain 5 years (AICPA) / 7 (PCAOB). After completion, add but don't delete (record reasons).
Risk-based firm system: governance/leadership, risk assessment, ethics, acceptance/continuance, engagement performance, resources, information/communication, monitoring/remediation.
Objective review by a qualified person NOT on the engagement, completed before the report is released; evaluates significant judgments and conclusions.
Responsible for overall engagement quality, direction, supervision, and review — the link between the firm's quality system and the individual audit.

questions.q: In a group audit, responsibility for the group audit opinion rests with:
questions.explain: The group engagement partner is responsible for the group opinion and the sufficiency of evidence.

questions.q: Before using the work of internal auditors, the external auditor must evaluate their:
questions.explain: AU-C 610 requires evaluating internal audit's competence and objectivity.

questions.q: Audit documentation should be sufficient for:
choices: An experienced auditor with no prior connection to understand the work
questions.explain: AU-C 230 sets the experienced-auditor understandability standard.

questions.q: For a non-issuer (AICPA) audit, the final documentation is assembled within:
questions.explain: AICPA documentation completion period is 60 days (PCAOB is 45).

questions.q: The AICPA's system of quality management is best described as:
choices: A risk-based system with quality objectives, risks, and responses
questions.explain: SQMS requires a risk-based system: set quality objectives, identify quality risks, design responses, and monitor.

questions.q: An engagement quality review must be completed:
choices: Only if the client requests it
questions.explain: The EQR by a non-team reviewer must be completed before releasing the report.

questions.q: Using a component auditor's work means the group auditor:
choices: Still retains responsibility for the sufficiency of evidence for the group opinion
Has no responsibility for that component
questions.explain: Delegating work is not delegating responsibility; the group team owns the sufficiency of evidence.
